 RAHUL GANDHI’S CLAIM DOESN’T MATCH THE DATA ❌

On June 17, 2026, at a rally in Rajasthan, Rahul Gandhi claimed that for every 1,000 young people entering the system:

• Only 36 would get permanent jobs

• Around 300 would remain unemployed

• Nearly 700 would become gig workers

But the official data paints a very different picture.

📊 A Bloomberg News analysis of unit-level PLFS data found that in 2025, 26 out of every 100 graduates aged 15–29 had regular salaried jobs.

Youth employment indicators have also improved:

➡️ Worker Population Ratio (15–29): 34.2% in 2013 → 41.4% in 2025

➡️ Unemployment rate: 7.71% in 2014 → 4.2% in 2025

And the claim that nearly 70% of young people will become gig workers has no credible data behind it.

NITI Aayog estimated 77 lakh gig workers in 2020–21, around 1.5% of India’s workforce, and projected this to reach about 4.1% of livelihoods by 2029–30.

36 permanent jobs + 300 unemployed + 700 gig workers?

The numbers simply don’t add up. ❌

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Section 16 of the DPDP Act lets the Government bar transfers of personal data to named countries. No country has been named, so personal data may leave India freely today.

The direction is the reverse of GDPR, which blocks transfers until a destination is approved. A section 16 notification needs no consultation and carries no transition period, and sectoral rules such as the RBI's payment data directive continue to apply regardless.

text:
🔆Telecommunications Bill 2023

✅Recently, the government introduced the Telecommunications Bill 2023 in the Lok Sabha. It seeks to repeal the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, the Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, and the Telegraph Wires (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1950. It also amends the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) Act, 1997.

📍What are the Key Provisions of Telecommunications Bill 2023?

✅Authorisation for Telecom-related Activities: Prior authorisation from the central government will be required to provide telecommunication services, establish, operate, maintain, or expand telecommunications networks, or possess radio equipment.
Existing licenses will continue to be valid for the period of their grant, or for five years, where the period is not specified.
✅Assignment of Spectrum: Spectrum will be assigned by auction, except for specified uses, where it will be allocated on an administrative basis. These include purposes such as national security and defense, disaster management, weather forecasting, transport, satellite services such as DTH and satellite telephony, and BSNL, MTNL, and public broadcasting services.
✅Satellite Internet Allotments: The Bill introduces provisions for allocating spectrum to satellite Internet providers like OneWeb (supported by Bharti) and U.S.-based companies such as SpaceX's Starlink.
✅Powers of Interception and Search: Messages or a class of messages between two or more persons may be intercepted, monitored, or blocked on certain grounds.
✅Powers to Specify Standards: The central government may prescribe standards and assessments for telecom equipment, infrastructure, networks, and services.
✅Right of Way: Facility providers may seek a right of way over public or private property to establish telecom infrastructure.
✅Appointments to TRAI: The Bill amends the TRAI Act to also allow individuals with: at least 30 years of professional experience to serve as the chairperson, and at least 25 years of professional experience to serve as members.
✅Digital Bharat Nidhi: The Universal Service Obligation Fund has been established under the 1885 Act to provide for telecom services in underserved areas.
✅Regulation of OTT Apps: It has removed over-the-top (OTT) services and apps from the definition of telecommunication services, in a big relief to communication service providers such as WhatsApp and Telegram.
✅Adjudication Process: The central government will appoint an adjudicating officer to conduct inquiries and pass orders against civil offenses under the Bill.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

A free press is not an ornament of democracy, it is its spine. As the fourth pillar, its constitutional duty is not to flatter power, but to interrogate it.
Under the Constitution of India, executive authority is neither absolute nor immune from scrutiny. Freedom of expression is not a privilege granted at the whim of the state,pĺit is a fundamental right forged to ensure those who govern remain answerable to those they govern.
When leaders dodge critical questions, silence scrutiny, or walk away from the microphone, it is not merely political evasion. It is an act of defiance against democratic accountability. It signals a dangerous premise, that power owes no explanation to the people.
Evasion is not strength,it is cowardice. A democracy rots when public servants/Ministers  treat public questioning as an inconvenience. Those who demand the authority to govern must have the courage to answer.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Information warfare has no rules, creating them is our next step — GFCN president
Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network
© Danil Aikin/TASS
Interview with Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network

President of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) Vladimir Tabak told TASS in an interview ahead of the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum about where most information attacks against Russia originate, how a disinformation campaign targeting elections to the State Duma is being prepared abroad, and which issues that are particularly sensitive to Russians are currently most vulnerable to fake news.

– Today we will be discussing a very important problem which, like a terrible disease, is capable of poisoning and replacing reality itself – fake news. And my first question to you is: which areas of Russians’ lives are being attacked by this disease first and foremost?

– It seems to me that today there are no areas that have escaped this disease. But if we are talking about the areas that are most vulnerable to it, those are everything related to security, political processes, and social issues. We know that there are currently certain fuel-related difficulties in the regions. There are also a large number of phishing websites offering fake fuel coupons, as well as unverified websites with completely bogus maps of gas stations that were created simply to collect users’ data. This is a vivid example of how a situation arising offline can prompt the creation of projects of this kind, which can then pose a fairly serious threat to citizens themselves and to the state, because systematic efforts against the country as a whole begin to take shape.

– When you hear all of this, it is hard not to feel a sense of hopelessness. Is there really nothing we can do to protect ourselves from this problem? Is there no antidote? Perhaps you could name some of the most effective methods of countering fake news?

– The situation with fake news is quite complicated today. We understand that there is a huge amount of cyber fraud. For me, even regardless of where I work, when 'a Sberbank representative' (a fake representative of Russia’s largest bank) connects you over the phone to 'an FSB representative' (a fake officer from Russia’s Federal Security Service), that is a somewhat strange situation. (This is a common scam tactic designed to gain the victim’s trust by making the call appear official – TASS). Or when an 'FSB representative' calls you on a video call, sitting in his office, and presents you with some kind of accusations.

But a huge number of people actually fall for this. On top of that, technologies are developing. There are deepfakes, for example. Today, 64% of people in surveys conducted by Dialogue Regions say that they know what deepfakes are. There were, of course, fewer of them before – 59% as of September 2025. At the same time, 80% overall say that they encounter unreliable information. What does that tell us? It tells us that we can focus exclusively on raising the population’s level of media literacy, creating an ecosystem of trust, and beyond that, it will still come down to personal responsibility, apart from situations where law enforcement agencies need to step in afterward. But at the moment when a person encounters one piece of information or another, the responsibility ultimately falls on the user.

This does not change the fact that we need to package and deliver our own information quickly and accurately. We need to be able to debunk disinformation that is spreading widely among a broad audience. In this sense, the state should not absolve itself of responsibility for, so to speak, organizing a large-scale process of informing people, debunking false information, providing education, and working with government agencies so that they, too, understand how to counter this. But given the scale at which this kind of information is being disseminated today, the only thing that can counter it on such a mass scale is a high level of media literacy and, ultimately, a basic degree of critical thinking on the part of users about what they are reading.

– The explosive growth in the amount of fake news has been driven by the development of artificial intelligence (AI). And there is currently a debate in many countries about mandatory labeling of content. Do you consider this a necessary measure? Perhaps you are in dialogue with government authorities or other organizations on this issue?

– At some point and to some extent, all countries will regulate this type of content. In fact, there are already pilot examples of countries where such content is being regulated. What is very important here is to find the right balance, because we understand that there are two opposite poles. At one end, AI helps reduce production costs and makes it possible to create content more quickly – it serves a positive function. And that function definitely should not get lost behind this bureaucratic process. At the other end, we have those same tools being deliberately used for destructive purposes. Here we need to find that delicate balance which, on the one hand, will allow legitimate content producers to continue operating in this market without unnecessary restrictions and, on the other hand, will create the right foundation for systematically countering those who use these technologies to cause harm.

Read also
From trendy toys to tools of political manipulation: rapid advancement of AI avatars
But the production landscape has also changed dramatically, if we can call it that. We understand that previously, this kind of content was primarily produced by small specialized groups, those who were themselves engaged in developing artificial intelligence. Today, technologies have reached a level at which this product has become mass-market, meaning that more than 50–60 percent of AI-generated content, for example, that you see on the internet is content created by users themselves. So, to answer the question you asked, a decision to introduce content labeling is inevitable in the foreseeable future.

– In a few days, we will have an important event – elections to the State Duma. This is probably a period of particularly high vulnerability to fake news. Are you seeing preparations for a disinformation campaign coming from outside the country? Through which channels, perhaps, are they planning to spread fake news, and what narratives will they target?

– There are classic approaches to delegitimizing the electoral process. These include videos related to the voting process itself. Even without taking any particular technologies into account, this could mean, for example, using old videos. I will give the most basic example: staged videos filmed at a polling station in order to convince the viewer that what they are seeing is happening here and now. This will certainly happen; we understand that.

Read also
False mobilization claims put society on edge ahead of Russian elections — GFCN chief
But there are also narratives that have nothing to do with the voting process itself – narratives intended to make this period more difficult for the authorities and for the country. And perhaps the most striking fake news story in this regard is the story about mobilization, which does not directly affect the elections. It could have an impact if mobilization were actually announced. But rumors about it undoubtedly create significant tension both among certain segments of the population and in society as a whole. And so, as you can see, even at the highest level, the Russian president addressed this issue, because the information really did spread extremely widely.

Obviously, there are opinion polls and there is analysis, but there is also a simple rule you can see in any personal chat group: if people you know start actively discussing a particular topic, then you know that topic is genuinely on people’s minds. I can say that this was discussed in every personal chat I am part of, and at every meeting I attended, someone asked a similar question. And it is clear that those who created and injected this fake news were relying on the idea that during the previous period, there was still a certain segment of people who became frightened and left, as well as the parents of those people, who were themselves under considerable stress. So, the objective pursued by our opponents is clear. I would identify this as one of the most prominent narratives we are observing.

– If it is possible to trace the source and, for example, make a list, a sort of tier list, of which countries carry out the most information attacks against Russia, what objectives are these countries pursuing?

– Ukraine is in first place, but this is fairly easy to explain. We are in a state of armed conflict, and today information warfare is part of the larger war. So, it would be strange if we were now talking about other countries dominating Ukraine in this regard. Ukraine has a separate unit, the Center for Information and Psychological Operations, or CIPsO, which is part of the regular armed forces and is classified as a military unit.

This is visible across many different issues. In other words, they get involved in any crisis-related topic and try to escalate it as much as possible and create additional tension around it. But at the same time, we understand that there are a number of countries that are also behaving quite aggressively and using specialized institutions to operate against us. First and foremost, this is Britain. This is a country that behaves quite aggressively in the information sphere. There are different methods. They have, so to speak, verified sources – media outlets and platforms that they support through various grant systems and through direct funding. There is also work involving AI, work targeting specific segments of the population, ranging from simple tactics in which certain issues are injected into the information space to more sophisticated operations.

But despite the fact that we are currently at a fairly acute stage of information confrontation, we should not discount ordinary people who often spread unreliable information without having any malicious intent. Again, this brings us back to the issue of cognitive awareness. Our task is to stop constantly saying that everything we see is somehow a product of our adversary. That is not the case. Fake news existed before. People tend, especially in situations when they feel uncertain or do not know the answers to questions that concern them, to come up with rather strange answers themselves, to put it politely, or to seek those answers in completely unverified sources. So here we need to work with the broader public so that people learn to verify information.

– So, what is needed is broad-based educational and explanatory work?

– Yes.

– Now let us talk about the association that you head. The Global Fact-Checking Network was established in 2025. Can you give us an interim assessment of this period? How has the nature of your activities, the scope of your tasks, and the scale of the network changed?

– First of all, I believe that the project has worked out overall. It is important to understand that this was initially a voluntary initiative. The project was created by us, by Russia’s News Agency TASS, and by the New Media Workshop. We created it amid the publicity surrounding our lawsuit against the FBI in the United States after we were accused of allegedly interfering in the US elections. And, to be completely honest, initially it was something of a PR move. But various industry participants from different countries showed interest, and today we have more than 125 journalists in the Association from 55 countries.

And every time at the forum (referring to the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum – TASS), more and more speakers and participants from different countries attend. The total number of guests at the forum has already exceeded 2,000–3,000, including Russian participants, but a significant share still comes from different countries, including countries that are currently considered unfriendly, yet there are journalists and media professionals there who are willing to engage with us.

We have released a number of interesting and high-profile investigations, and we have developed a substantial educational program. Several memoranda have been adopted at major international events based on the GFCN Code of Responsible Fact-Checking. Some provisions of our Code were also included in the final statement of the 12th BRICS Communications Ministers’ Meeting at the recent summit in India. And today we have begun working quite closely with colleagues from China and Kazakhstan. A GFCN expert was in Kazakhstan during the elections as part of the CIS observation mission, and before that our representatives were in Venezuela. Again, we are invited to participate in various events, and it is important to understand that GFCN currently has no funding of any kind. In other words, we are essentially participants and members who have other, primary jobs, and for whom this is, as our opponents like to put it, a "guilty pleasure."

So, as a project created entirely on enthusiasm, I think the Network has exceeded my expectations in any case. On about five or six occasions already, the International Fact-Checking Network, a fact-checking association funded by the Poynter Institute, has mentioned in its articles that we are a lying Kremlin propaganda network. I consider that a great success. So, when I compare the resources invested with the results, I am very pleased with the work of the Network.

– We have already mentioned information adversaries. As allies, as I understand it, you have named China and Kazakhstan?

– There are actually many countries. We are currently integrating closely with the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies (OANA), which is currently chaired by TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov. So this includes Asia, the Pacific, Latin American countries, and CIS countries. Some show greater interest, others less. We are as open as possible here. We have an educational section on our website, which already contains more than 170 articles and videos covering various areas of fact-checking, media literacy, and OSINT tools (open-source intelligence research – TASS), all of which are available to users on the website. Our position here is quite open. We are not claiming ideological leadership; rather, we want to bring together people who are interested in this field. So, some countries show more active interest, and there are individual representatives of countries who are particularly active. But I would say that as this issue becomes increasingly relevant, interest will continue to grow.

– You have touched on the Network’s educational role. In your view, what qualities need to be cultivated among young journalists, fact-checkers, and researchers? What do you pay particular attention to, and what are you trying to develop?

– There is an expression: an inquisitive mind. I think that is the most important thing. I was personally the driving force behind launching this initiative, but I am not an OSINT specialist (a professional who collects, analyzes, and interprets information from publicly available sources – TASS) and I am not a fact-checker (a professional who specializes in verifying the accuracy of information – TASS) myself. What matters to me is creating a certain atmosphere for this "community" and giving it an opportunity to grow. And when I look at people who, in my view and in the view of my colleagues, have that kind of fact-checking talent, they are extremely inquisitive. They are meticulous, perhaps even somewhat distrustful at times, but I think people like that could work very well in law enforcement agencies.

I am exaggerating a little, of course, but you need to be appropriately skeptical. We are not talking about some kind of blind or irrational distrust. You need to start from the assumption that we live in a very difficult information environment filled with millions of unverified sources. At the same time, the internet now gives us the ability to verify an enormous amount of information without resorting to any closed or restricted verification methods. The ability to think critically on the one hand and to use these tools on the other, taken together, gives us an excellent synergy for helping these talented people grow and develop.

– From everything we have discussed, it already seems that fact-checking has ceased to be primarily a tool for journalists. Can we say that it has now become a distinct international area of cooperation? And what kind of global model for interaction would you perhaps propose?

– It is difficult for me to say what a global model of cooperation would look like, but I have thought, for example, about the fact that there are conventional rules governing warfare. If those rules are violated, there is a regulatory body where sanctions or consequences for such actions are considered. For example, is inducing a teenager to commit murder or arson as part of information warfare essentially the same thing as using cluster munitions in a conventional war? I believe it is. Because that goes beyond the bounds of information confrontation in the sense in which I see and understand it. And in my view, even if today we are talking about us and our adversaries with whom we are waging this information war, there still need to be certain rules. Unfortunately, as of today, there is no such framework for defining those rules. It would be quite difficult to establish it at the global level right now. We understand the geopolitical situation, especially if we were, so to speak, the ones initiating such an effort. But in my view, these rules need to emerge. And that is the next step.

But globally, despite all the popularity and hype surrounding fact-checking, it has still not become a fundamental part of journalism. And we need to understand that journalism itself has also undergone a transformation. As a graduate of the journalism faculty at Moscow State University, I can say that journalism today and journalism even 15 years ago are completely different fields, and today many major publications are facing the question of how they can continue to exist, because modern media consumption and the monetization of platforms that results from it seem not to provide for their presence on anything close to the same scale.

So, the question here is not how fact-checking will be incorporated into journalism; the broader question is what will happen to journalism itself in the coming years. And fact-checking, in my view, is not purely a journalistic field. At a basic everyday level, it is something that every adult today should possess at least minimal skills in for their own safety. At the professional level, it involves groups of ordinary people who work in the interests of private companies, in the interests of the state, and in their own interests, if they are investigators or people working in related fields.

– I will be completely candid: it is very interesting to listen to you, and it makes me want to delve deeper into these issues. On September 22, we have a major event coming up – the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum, which will provide an opportunity to discuss all of this in greater detail.

– Yes, we will have presentations there, and we are very grateful to the Russian Foreign Ministry for supporting the forum throughout all these years. Without the Foreign Ministry, we certainly would not have been able to put together an event on this scale. And this year, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov will personally take part in the forum. We are very grateful to him for responding to our requests. And we are also grateful to Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Vladimirovna Zakharova for her endless, consistent support.

– This is the fourth time the forum has been held. What will make this year special? What topics will be the key ones?

– I do not like talking about any particular forum as being special, because then we somewhat diminish the value of the previous forums that came before it. In my view, the community is simply becoming larger, stronger, and broader. Again, new international projects of a higher level are emerging, and negotiations with a number of countries are also moving to a new level. For me, this is a way to formalize agreements – in some cases in an official setting, in others in an informal one – and once again to draw centralized attention to the issue that my colleagues at "Dialogue," our partners, and I have been working on for several years now.

– And what are you expecting in terms of scale?

– Every year, our forum is larger than the previous one. And this year we will have more participants than we did last year. So, in terms of scale, yes, it will be bigger. But the issue is not the number of participants; first and foremost, we look at the level of representation and the standing of the experts taking part. That is also higher than in previous years, and this is a significant result for us.

– We will be looking forward to it. Thank you very much for the interview.

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia 

#Samsung #SamsungIndia #GalaxyS25Ultra #SamsungService #Nagpur #ConsumerRights #scamservice

🚨 SONY CROSSED A LINE. 

I’ve criticized Sony over PlayStation, digital ownership, pricing & physical media, but this story is on another level.

A customer in India bought a ₹1.5 lakh (350 US) Sony Bravia with a three-year Sony warranty. About 22 months later, vertical lines started across the display.

He contacted Sony.

According to the documented case, Sony’s tech came to the home, photographed the television, and those pics were sent through WhatsApp to a backend team. Sony eventually classified the problem as “external damage,” denied warranty coverage and quoted the customer ₹29,130 ($2771)  for the repair.

The customer asked reasonable question:

SHOW ME THE DAMAGE.

Where is the crack, dent, the impact point? What test determined this was external damage?

He says Sony never produced the evidence he was asking for.

So he documented everything..

And THIS is where it goes from a warranty claim to something we should be paying attention to.

Sony India’s lawyers sent him a legal notice demanding that he remove his videos, posts and website and issue an unconditional apology within seven days. The notice warned that Sony could pursue civil and criminal proceedings, including monetary damages of AT LEAST ₹5 CRORE. 
($ 525,558.50)

Half a million dollars. +/-
Think about that.
A customer buys your television.
The television fails while covered by your warranty.

Sony denied the warranty.

The customer publicly challenges Sony's explanation and asks them to prove the damage.

Instead of ending this whole mess by putting the technical evidence on the table, lawyers threaten with hundreds of thousands of dollars.

What the hell are we doing here?

And sadly, this story isn't happening in a vacuum.

Sony introduced a customer-harassment policy in Japan that allows it to terminate support and potentially pursue legal action in serious cases involving abusive conduct. Protecting employees from genuine threats and harassment is reasonable. Nobody should have to tolerate threats.

But we have every right to question companies, dispute decisions, demand refunds if appropriate, complain to regulators and publicly criticize a corporation.

The lines CAN'T be allowed to become  blurred.

Then look at PlayStation.

Reports show different PSN accounts receiving dramatically different discounts for the SAME games. Sony is experimenting with account-based or dynamic pricing, with factors behind those differences still not completely transparent.

Now put this together.
More control over digital games.
Less physical ownership.
A storefront Sony controls.
Different customers seeing different discounts.

Policies giving Sony dystopian tools for dealing with customer conduct.

And now a documented case where Sony's lawyers threaten a warranty customer with enormous damages after he publicly challenged their decision.

At what point does the customer stop being the CUSTOMER and start becoming someone the corporation believes needs to be managed?

This is why Ethica Gaming talks about consumer ownership and consumer leverage.

This isn't simply “Sony bad.”

This is what happens when a corporation controls the product, the warranty decision, the digital storefront, the pricing, your account and increasingly the rules governing how you interact with them.

Power without competition or consumer leverage should concern EVERY gamer regardless of what plastic box sits underneath your television.

Huge kudos @Jacson for researching this and putting the pieces together. This is the kind of consumer reporting we need more of.

Watch it
https://t.co/abX6T1ImZM

Watch the evidence. Look at the documents. Decide for yourself.

Whether you're buying a $1,500 television or an $80 digital game, there is one principle corporations seem to keep forgetting:

WE'RE THE CUSTOMERS.

Not an inconvenience.

@Sony @PlayStation @Jacson @PaulTassi @MysticRyan @LUCKYY10P @Aztecross @Blaze2k

#Sony #PlayStation #PS

UPDATE 
UPDATE!!!

Three grown men connected with this takeaway have just come to my home following my post.

For the avoidance of doubt, if anything happens to my house, car or property, the police have already been made aware of tonight’s incident.

Three grown men turning up at a woman’s home after she has raised concerns publicly is extremely intimidating.

He told me that the man involved was an employee and assured me that he would be sacked.

text:
Hackers took everything on all my Phantom wallets. 
Because @AppStore lets you download a fake @AxiomExchange wallet !!!!!!!!!!

From Grok:
This matches a known scam. There is no official Axiom iOS app. The real Axiom product is a browser/PWA site. Fake App Store listings using names like “Axiom Pro” have been used to steal Solana wallet seed phrases and drain funds. App Store reviews for at least one listing describe exactly that: the app asked for a recovery phrase, then the wallet was emptied.23
Do these steps in order.
1. Stop the app
•Delete Axiom Pro now: long-press the icon → Remove App → Delete App.
•Check Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. Remove any unknown configuration profile.
•Restart the iPhone.
An App Store app on a non-jailbroken iPhone usually cannot take over the whole phone the way PC malware can. The usual damage here is crypto theft if you typed a seed phrase, private key, or approved a wallet connection—not full iOS control.
2. Treat any wallet you used in that app as burned
If you entered a seed phrase / recovery phrase, imported a wallet, or signed anything in that app:
•Do not send more money to that wallet.
•From a different device (or after deleting the app), create a brand-new wallet with a new seed phrase.
•Move any remaining assets out of the old wallet to the new one as soon as you can.
•Revoke token approvals on the old wallet if anything is left (use a trusted revoke tool from a clean device).
Anyone who already has the seed phrase can keep draining that wallet later. Changing a password on the same seed does not fix it.
3. Lock down accounts
On another device if possible:
•Change your Apple ID password and check Settings → [your name] for unknown devices / purchases.
•Change email password and turn on 2FA.
•Check bank, cards, PayPal, and other crypto wallets/exchanges for unauthorized activity.
•Enable 2FA everywhere (authenticator app, not SMS if you can).
4. Report it
•Report the app to Apple: https://t.co/oFb32Z5H19
•If crypto was stolen, report to local police and keep transaction hashes. Recovery of on-chain theft is rare.
5. Ignore “recovery” helpers
People will DM offering to “trace” or “recover” funds. That is almost always a second scam.

Tell me only what you did in the app (no seed phrase, no private key):
•Did it ask you to type a 12/24-word phrase?
•Did you connect Phantom or another wallet?
•Did any SOL/tokens actually leave?
With that I can tell you whether this is mainly “delete the app and change passwords” or “abandon that wallet immediately.”

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

20. Cargo Ship Fire Kills 25 in Qingdao
A front-page report in Statesman says a cargo ship docked for repairs at the Beihai Shipbuilding Co. in Qingdao caught fire, killing 25 people. Chinese state media reported Thursday that President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang ordered urgent rescue operations. Of the 42 people on board, 12 were safely evacuated and five injured remained in stable condition.
Why it matters: Port safety protocols and emergency response capabilities are under scrutiny following a major maritime tragedy.
Key detail: A blaze aboard a foreign-flagged bulk carrier docked at Beihai Shipbuilding Co. resulted in 25 fatalities out of 42 crew members, prompting urgent state-level rescue directives.

Next step: Terminal operators must audit fire suppression systems and conduct mandatory crew safety drills ahead of peak season.

9. Supreme Court Questions Delhi Metro Closures
A front-page report in The Pioneer says the Supreme Court has issued a notice to the Union of India and Delhi Police over the closure of seventeen metro stations during July protests at Jantar Mantar. A three-judge bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana heard the plea filed by advocate Sparsh Kant Nayak, which challenges the sudden shutdown as a violation of public constitutional rights. The court directed all concerned authorities to submit their responses regarding the disruption of essential public transport services.
Why it matters: Judicial oversight on public transport accessibility sets a precedent for urban mobility rights during civic disruptions.
Key detail: The bench directed the central government, Delhi Police, and DMRC to justify the shutdown of 17 stations during July protests, noting vehicle regulation falls under police jurisdiction.
Source: Times of India
Next step: Transit authorities should align operational continuity plans with constitutional mandates on public access.

14. Gadkari Warns Contractors Over Mumbai-Goa Highway Delays
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says Gaonkars in Bhoma are demanding no highway widening or flyover through their village, protecting the settlement, and building a bypass to divert through traffic away from Bhoma. Union road transport minister Gadkari is pushing for two major projects totaling around Rs 6,000 crore, while six road projects have yet to begin due to pending tree-cutting permissions.
Why it matters: Government accountability measures directly impact national highway completion timelines and contractor compliance standards.
Key detail: Union Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari threatened blacklisting for negligent contractors and officials, planning an October ground inspection to enforce a perform-or-perish framework.
Source: First India
Next step: Project managers must accelerate milestone deliveries and maintain transparent progress reporting to avoid regulatory penalties.

5. SpiceJet Shares Fall as Government Monitors Financials
A front-page report in Millennium Post says the Indian government and civil aviation regulator DGCA are closely monitoring budget carrier SpiceJet due to significant financial strains and declining domestic market share. Civil Aviation Minister K Rammohan Naidu confirmed the oversight on Thursday following reports that staff salaries have remained unpaid since May, while the airline domestic market share fell to one point six per cent in July. Despite finalising lease agreements for twenty leased aircraft for the upcoming winter schedule, SpiceJet shares dipped five point three two per cent to close at eight rupees and eighty nine paise.
Why it matters: Regulatory scrutiny on budget carriers signals tighter oversight of airline solvency and fleet sustainability.
Key detail: Civil Aviation Minister K Rammohan Naidu confirmed DGCA monitoring after staff salaries went unpaid since May and domestic market share slipped to 1.6 percent, despite securing leases for 20 aircraft.
Source: Millennium Post
Next step: Investors and partners should track quarterly liquidity reports and route profitability metrics closely.

2. 5.6% Drop in Domestic Airline Capacity
A front-page report in Financial Express says that India's domestic airline capacity fell 5.6% to 22.7 million seats in September compared to 23.8 million a year earlier. Airlines are prioritising profitable routes such as Mumbai-Delhi, which saw a 13.9% increase, while cutting capacity on other city pairs like Mumbai-Hyderabad and Mumbai-Chennai. The reduction is driven by higher aviation turbine fuel costs, international airspace disruptions, and constrained aircraft availability for carriers like SpiceJet.
Why it matters: Carrier capacity rationalization reflects broader economic pressures and fuel cost volatility in the aviation sector.
Key detail: September domestic seats fell to 22.7 million from 23.8 million year-earlier, with airlines prioritizing high-yield Mumbai-Delhi routes while trimming Mumbai-Hyderabad and Chennai frequencies.
Source: Financial Express
Next step: Freight forwarders and travel agencies should anticipate schedule adjustments and book cargo space early on core corridors.

1. Nashik Gets 1,435 Km Road Network
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says preparations for the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027 are driving a massive 1,435.81 km road infrastructure programme across Nashik and Trimbakeshwar. Multiple agencies, including the NHAI, PWD, and local municipal bodies, are developing the network to accommodate pilgrim influxes while integrating essential utilities like drainage and fibre optics for long-term urban development. The expanded transport corridor aims for completion by March 2027 to significantly ease congestion and boost regional connectivity beyond the religious festival.
Why it matters: Regional infrastructure expansion directly supports pilgrimage traffic management and long-term urban connectivity.
Key detail: NHAI, PWD, and municipal bodies are accelerating a 1,435.81 km network integrating drainage and fibre optics, targeting March 2027 completion to ease congestion beyond the Simhastha Kumbh Mela.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Local logistics providers should prepare fleet deployment strategies aligned with the new corridor openings.

24. Mundra Port Operations Resume After Strike
A front-page report in Financial Express says empty yard container operators on Thursday called off their thirteen-day old strike against Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone's decision to freeze empty yard codes located outside the port and SEZ limits. Mundra Empty Container Yards and Allied Services Provider Association told stakeholders in an internal communication that it has decided to resume operations with immediate effect. Operations resumed from ten a.m. and a detailed trade advisory would be issued shortly.
Why it matters: Labor resolution at India’s largest private port restores critical empty yard container flows and supply chain predictability.
Key detail: Operators ended a 13-day standoff over frozen yard codes outside SEZ limits, resuming full trade advisory processes and terminal movements from 10 a.m. Thursday.

A front-page report in Free Press Journal says veteran human resources professional Dr Santosh Bhave urges organisations to foster intergenerational collaboration rather than viewing Generation Z and older workers as competitors. He highlighted the need for leadership to shift towards coaching, listening, and open trust during his address at the National Institute of Personnel Management lecture in Mumbai. 16. DGCA Orders Drug Tests For Pilots
A front-page report in First India says the DGCA has ordered drug tests for pilots across all airlines to be completed by July 2027. Civil Aviation Minister K Rammohan Naidu stated the draft on new norms for psychoactive substance testing will be finalised by the end of this month. The move follows a pilot-in-command of an Air India Phuket-Delhi flight testing positive for drug use after the aircraft suddenly lost nearly 300 feet altitude on August 4, injuring many passengers.

text:
BREAKING: Revolut handed over passports and Bitcoin records after a fake government request

Revolut has confirmed that customer files left the company after staff treated a fraudulent request for information as genuine. The message did not come from just a lookalike email address. It came from an unauthorised mailbox on a real government domain and passed the usual email checks. Because it looked official, Revolut sent the data. Only later, after contacting the agency itself, did the firm realise the request was bogus.

The files listed in customer notices go well beyond a name and an email. They include full name, date of birth, occupation, home address, phone number, copies of passports or driving licences, the verification selfie taken at sign-up, IBANs, account statements, withdrawal records and full transaction histories, including Bitcoin. Revolut says biometric face templates, login details and customer funds were not involved. Its systems were not hacked. No money is reported to have moved.

A spokesperson told @BeInCrypto the company had identified “a sophisticated external impersonation attack where an unauthorised third party utilised a legitimate government agency domain email to submit fraudulent requests for information.” The same statement said Revolut’s systems and customer funds were unaffected. The firm says it blocked the sender, alerted the agency, the police and regulators, and contacted what it called a limited number of people. It has not named the agency or said how many customers were affected, citing a live police investigation. On-chain investigator @zachxbt , who first circulated the notices, said the incident looked small and aimed at higher-value users.

A post circulating on X claimed a Revolut employee in charge of data security had just been sacked after asking whether the “.gov” address should be verified first. I understand that post is a parody. No evidence shows such a sacking took place.

One person who contacted me knows someone who received the Revolut notice. At the time of writing, they could not provide details of how the company had communicated with that customer beyond the existence of the email.

I understand this was human error in a process that assumes an authenticated government domain is enough. That assumption failed. It is an uncomfortable reminder that the most sensitive files a firm holds — identity documents, a face photo, a home address and a complete payment history — can leave the building without anyone breaking in. Any company that stores that pile and answers official-looking demands can make the same mistake. The test is whether Revolut, and everyone else sitting on the same kind of records, starts checking the person behind the mailbox, not just the domain on the envelope.

Foreign VPNs have often been found involved in planning & execution of terror activities, funding, facilitation and radicalisation of youth and crime against children & women by spread of p€rverted content & therefore the biggest threat to the nation's security and culture. Below is my letter to GOI seeking an immediate ban on foreign VPNs & detailing instances of their blatant misuse for:

A. Terrorism and radicalisation
B. Crime against children and women
C. Financial fraud
D. Drug trafficking
E. Extortion, blackmailing, etc.

In my letter I have listed a sample of 50 serious instances of these crimes and terror activities from India and around the world.

Below is the full text of the letter :

10th November 2025

Shri Amit Shah
Union Home Minister

Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw
Union Minister of Electronics and Information Technology

Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal
Union Minister of State (I/C) for Law & Justice

Smt Annpurna Devi
Union Minister of Women and Child Development

Sub: Urgent Request for Immediate Nationwide Ban on Foreign VPN Services to Curb Crimes Against Children, Women, Drug Trafficking, Financial Fraud, and Threats to National Security

Dear Shri Amit Shah Ji,

Namaste.

I write as a concerned citizen to bring to your urgent attention the direct role of foreign VPN services in enabling heinous crimes against children, women, and acts of terrorism—crimes that are actively bypassing existing Indian laws. Section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, via directions issued on 28 April 2022, imposes a mandatory 5-year logging requirement on VPN providers.

Despite the mandatory 5-year logging requirement imposed on VPN providers under these directions, major foreign VPNs—NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark, ProtonVPN, Mullvad, and others—have openly refused compliance by removing physical servers from India and routing traffic through virtual IPs abroad. This deliberate non-cooperation has turned these services into safe havens for criminals and terrorists operating in and targeting India.

For example, the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog, Financial Action Task Force (FATF), reported on July 8, 2025, that the accused in two recent terror attacks in India—the Gorakhnath Temple attack in Uttar Pradesh on April 3, 2022, and the Pulwama suicide-bomb attack in February 2019, which killed 40 CRPF personnel—used online payment services, e-commerce platforms, and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).

The list of crimes and terror-related incidents involving VPNs is long. We are listing below just a few recent examples of how VPNs were used to commit crimes against children and women, plan terrorist activities, traffic drugs and conduct fraud. Each incident lists the crime, VPN use, and primary-source link [U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) / Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) / European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) / The International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol)].

Crimes Against Children (VPN-Enabled Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) Cases)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs (or VPN + Tor) to hide while committing Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) related crimes—downloading, sharing, or live-streaming.

1. Connecticut, USA – 2025
Michael Hull (61) used paid VPN + Tor for 4 years to access dark-web CSAM. FBI traced via VPN IP leak → DOJ
2. Minnesota, USA – Operation Grayskull, 2025
Thomas Katsampes (52) ran a 2,000-user CSAM forum requiring VPN + Tor hopping. FBI de-anonymized 18 admins via logs → DOJ
3. Florida, USA – Playpen Network, 2023–2025
956 arrests; 214 used NordVPN/PIA/Mullvad + Tor. FBI NIT malware captured real IPs on CSAM clicks → FBI
4. Germany – Boystown Takedown, 2021 (ongoing 2023 arrests)
400,000 users; rules mandated VPN + Tor. BKA arrested 72; 2 VPN providers surrendered logs under EU warrants → BKA/Europol
5. South Korea – Welcome to Video, 2019–2024
337 arrests; 41 used VPN exits in Sweden/Romania for Bitcoin CSAM buys. IRS traced VPN payments → DOJ
6. Australia – Childs Play, 2016–2017 (2023 follow-ups)
1.1M users; admin taught 3-VPN chaining + Tor. Task Force Argos caught 94 via VPN leaks → Queensland Police
7. Latin America – Operation Vibora, 2025
20 arrests; suspects used free mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder) for live-streamed child rape. VPN logs seized → Interpol
8. Oklahoma, USA – Thomas Gailus, 2025
Repeat offender used dark web via VPN to collect CSAM of prepubescents. 10-year sentence → DOJ
9. Washington, USA – Operation Restore Justice, 2025
Mitchell Dufault distributed CSAM via VPN-masked platforms. 10-year sentence → DOJ
10. Arizona, USA – 22 Defendants, 2023–2025
Multiple offenders used VPNs for CSAM possession/distribution. Charges under Project Safe Childhood → DOJ

Crimes Against Women (VPN-Enabled Cyberstalking/Sextortion)

Here are 10 cases where offenders used VPNs for cyberstalking, sextortion, or non-consensual porn against women.

1. Massachusetts, USA – James Florence Jr, 2025
Cyberstalked 13 women with paid VPNs for deepfake nudes/rape threats. 9-year sentence → DOJ
2. Albuquerque, USA – Phillip Gonzales, 2025
Sent rape-fantasy texts to 7 women via VPN-chained VoIP. VPN logs seized → DOJ
3. Global – 911 S5 Botnet, 2025
YunHe Wang sold VPN-proxied IPs for 4,000+ sextortion/rape threats against women. Servers seized → DOJ
4. Los Angeles, USA – Kody Roberts, 2023
Sent rape/murder threats to 3 women via commercial VPN. NIT grabbed IP → DOJ
5. Florida, USA – Christopher Buonocore, 2021–2024
Sextorted dozens, hired rapists via NordVPN + Tor. Bitcoin traces led to arrest → DOJ
6. Washington DC, USA – Nahvarj Mills, 2024
Posted revenge porn via Swedish VPN exits. 27-count indictment → DOJ
7. Naperville, USA – Cody Ratliff, 2025
Sextorted teen girl via mobile VPNs (Turbo/Thunder). Logs handed over → Police
8. California, USA – Chavarri Sextortion, 2019–2021 (2025 arrest)
Stalked/harassed women via VPN-masked accounts for nudes → DOJ
9. Global – Financial Sextortion Surge, 2023–2025
Overseas offenders used VPNs for anonymous threats; 33.5M losses → FinCEN/FBI
10. Nigeria – Operation Artemis, 2025
22 arrests for sextortion using VPNs to mask ops; 54K teen victims → FBI

Terrorism (VPN-Enabled Plots/Propaganda)

Here are 10 cases where terrorists used VPNs for propaganda, recruitment, or planning.

1. ISIS Global Propaganda – 2024
9 admins ran 150+ servers with https://t.co/hZjw1LIHqM mandatory. FBI/Europol seized; logs exposed → FBI/Europol
2. Terrorgram Collective – 2024
Leaders used Mullvad + Tor for kill lists/bomb manuals. Payment slip traced → DOJ
3. Al-Qaeda Inspire Distributors – 2023–2025

4. Hamas Crypto-Fundraising – 2025
3 operatives laundered $2M via DoubleVPN Sweden exits. Logs identified wallets → DOJ

Abdelhamid Hassan uploaded 200+ videos via Safe-Inet VPN. Logs showed 18 US IPs → DOJ
6. The Base Bomb Cell – Germany/USA, 2024
5 neo-Nazis plotted via Insorg VPN C2. Logs named all → DOJ/Europol
7. Hamas Live-Stream Recruiters – Spain, 2025
9 operatives streamed via VPN-chained apps. Turbo VPN logs revealed 73 → Eurojust
8. EU Jihadist Plots – 2023–2024
24 plots (6 attacks) used VPNs for online radicalization post-Hamas Oct 7 → Europol TE-SAT
9. Al-Qaeda Online Jihad – 2023
Propaganda surge via VPN-masked uploads after Zawahiri death → Europol
10. Hamas/Al-Qassam Finance – 2025
3 campaigns dismantled; VPNs obscured cyber-finance for arms → DOJ

Other Serious Threats (VPN-Enabled Ransomware/Fraud/Etc.)

Here are 10 cases of VPN use in ransomware, hacks, fraud, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking (no overlap with prior categories).

1. ALPHV/BlackCat – US Firms, 2023
3 hackers used Mullvad/ProtonVPN for $5M ransomware. Wallet traced → DOJ
2. LockBit Hospital Attacks – TX/CA, 2024
